How the index works
Facts have sources
 21,449 sources behind 999 listings. Select any dotted-underlined fact on a tool page to see the sentence we read, where, and when.
Makers can claim, not rank
 A verified maker can keep the description, screenshots, links and pricing current. Their facts are marked as theirs. Score, rank, votes and quotes are out of reach.
The weights are published
 Hacker News mindshare, the same for open and closed tools. GitHub stars are shown beside it, not mixed in. Votes can only raise a score: up to 20% of it reflects upvotes, graded on a curve against the most-voted tool. The square-root curve has a floor of 100 effective votes. Votes decay with a 90-day half-life. Maker self-votes do not count. Counts below 10 are hidden for display only. How the score is built 
Sponsors are labeled
 Sponsored placements say who paid and are never a row in a ranked list. Rankings pages carry none. No affiliate links. Rules and prices 
ADE Index ADE Index, the index of agentic development environments, is made by the team behind atrium . atrium is listed and scored like every other tool. Read the owner disclosure.

author: sidcraftscode
body:

The 7-Day Virtual Model Home for builders
Sell your plans before you build them.
A virtual model home buyers can walk through on their phone, built from the floor plans you already sell from. Every room in 360, live within 7 days of approving finishes.
Get your free demo room → 
 How it works 
Send one floor plan. See your own room in 360 within 48 hours. Free, no deposit.

Plan

01 How it works
Your own room first. Then the whole home in 7 days.
No new drawings, no software and no contract to see it. Send one plan PDF and judge the result on your own house type, before you spend anything. How a floor plan becomes a 360 tour .
STEP 1 Send one plan PDF
 Email the floor plan of a house type you’re selling now and tell us which room to start with. Add finish specs or photos if you have them, or let us suggest a style.
STEP 2 Your demo room in 48 hours
 We build that room from your own plan as a 360 scene, with your name on it, and send you a private link. Free, with no deposit and nothing to sign.
STEP 3 A 15-minute call
 If you like what you see, we talk through the full model home, what’s included and a quote for your plan. You pay in full up front, before we build. No deposit, no subscription.
STEP 4 Live within 7 days
 Approve your finishes and the whole home is live within 7 days: on your website, with a link for Zillow and MLS and a QR sign for the lot. Add finish options or the rest of your catalogue whenever you’re ready.
02 What you get
Everything you need to sell the plan, done for you.
One plan in, a complete virtual model home out. No software to learn, no logins, nothing to host.
The full 360 tour Every room of the home in 6K 360, with room-to-room moves, a floor-plan map, and full support for phones and tablets. Core 
Listing photo pack Stills pulled from the same scenes, ready for Zillow, MLS and Rightmove, brochures and sales boards. Included 
Website and portal setup We put the tour on your website for you, and give you a link to use on listing portals. Included 
QR sign file A print-ready QR sign for the lot, so passers-by can walk the home from the street. Included 
Social reel A 30-second vertical walkthrough video for Instagram, Facebook and TikTok. Included 
12 months of hosting The tour stays live and fast for the first year at no extra cost. Included 
A furnished model home ties up a house and tens of thousands in furniture. A virtual one is ready in a week, and works for every buyer who looks at that plan, on every lot.
Accuracy guarantee
If any room doesn’t match the plan you sent, we fix it free, as many times as it takes.
Speed
Live in 7 days from when you approve finishes.
03 What buyers get
A plan they can stand inside.
A floor plan asks buyers to imagine the house. A virtual model home lets them look around it, at eye level, from wherever they are.
Walk room to room
Move from the front door to the back garden at their own pace, with a floor-plan map to see how the rooms connect.
Works on their phone
Opens in the browser on a phone, tablet or laptop. No app, no download, no headset.
Open day, every day
On your website, on listing portals, from a QR sign at the lot, or in a follow-up after a call. The model home never closes.
04 For builders who sell from a plan catalogue
One virtual model home per plan. Every lot covered.
If you sell the same plans across lots and communities, each virtual model home keeps working for every buyer who looks at that house type. More about virtual model homes for builders and virtual show homes for UK new builds .
Regional and production builders Sell a plan before a model home exists, or for plans you’ll never build a model for. 
 Custom builders and plan designers Let buyers walk a design before they commit to the build or the plan set. 
 ADU and modular firms Help homeowners picture a unit on their lot before they go ahead. 
Your whole catalogue
Every house type, done at once.
Start with one plan. When you’re ready, we build every house type in your catalogue in one go, at catalogue rates per plan, then add extra finish options or colour schemes as you need them.
Ask about your catalogue 
05 FAQ
Questions builders ask.
What do I need to send you? The floor plan PDF for a house type you’re selling, and which room you’d like as your demo room. Elevations, photos of finished homes and finish specs help us match your look, but they’re optional. If anything on the drawings is unclear, we’ll ask.
 How long does it take? Your demo room within 48 hours of receiving a clear plan. The full tour is live within 7 days of you approving finishes. If something on the drawings needs checking, we ask first and the clock starts once we have what we need.
 What does it cost, and when do I pay? The demo room is free. There’s no deposit and nothing to commit to. If you want the full virtual model home, we quote per plan, with catalogue rates when you have several house types, and you pay in full before we build it.
 What if a room doesn’t match my plan? That’s our accuracy guarantee: if any room doesn’t match the plan you sent, we fix it free, as many times as it takes.
 Can you do our whole catalogue? Yes. Most builders start with one plan, then we build every house type at once, at catalogue rates. Extra finish options or colour schemes can be added per plan later.
 Is the tour an exact picture of the finished home? It’s an artist’s impression built from your plans. The layout follows your drawings; furniture, decor and landscaping are there to help buyers picture living in it.
 What happens to our plans? We use them only to build your demo room and, if you go ahead, your tours. They aren’t shared, sold, published or used for anyone else’s work. Demo rooms sit behind private links until you choose to share them. See our privacy page .
 Do buyers need an app or a headset? No. The tour opens from a link in any modern browser, on a phone, tablet or computer.
 Where are you based? London. We work with builders in the US and the UK.
06 Get started
Send one plan. See your own room in 360.
Pick a house type you’re selling now and tell us which room to start with. Within 48 hours you’ll get a private link to that room, built from your plan with your name on it. Free, no deposit.

title: Show HN: Lazycow Studio – turns footage you never edited into reels, locally
author: kensaurus
body:
# kensaurus/lazycow-studio Your footage, made into reels and trip films on your own computer. You only press Approve. MCP + API + npm. By kensaurus. - Stars: 0 - Forks: 0 - Watchers: 0 - Open issues: 0 - License: Apache License 2.0 - Homepage: https://kensaur.us - Default branch: main - Created: 2026-11-13T03:19:04Z ## Languages - Batchfile - HTML - JavaScript - PowerShell - Python - Shell - TypeScript ## Topics - ai-agents - claude - content-creation - local-first - mcp - mcp-server - model-context-protocol - open-source - reels - remotion - self-hosted - social-media-automation - video-editing - youtube-shorts ## Top Contributors - kensaurus (6 contributions) --- ## README # Lazycow Studio **You shot it. Lazycow edits it.** Licence: Apache-2.0 npm: lazycow MCP registry: io.github.kensaurus/lazycow Latest release The footage you never edited becomes reels and trip films. You only press **Approve**. Lazycow Studio finds the right clips in your photos and videos, cuts short vertical reels on the beat of free music, and builds long YouTube videos in parts, with maps and chapters. Then it books the posts. It runs on your own computer. Lazycow Studio is made by **kensaurus**. It is free and open source under Apache-2.0. - **Your footage stays on your computer.** Tagging and search run on your own processor. The studio only reads your files. Nothing leaves your computer unless you connect a network or add a key for a paid AI tool. - **A person approves every post.** Nothing is booked or posted until you press **Approve**. AI agents can make drafts and post approved reels. They cannot approve. - **Your AI agent can drive it.** An MCP server, an HTTP API (OpenAPI) and an npm package. One line connects Claude Code, Claude Desktop or Cursor. **Who it is for:** a small hotel, guesthouse, café or shop, or a creator, with a folder of footage and no time to edit it. You do not need to code: download, unzip, double-click. It posts to YouTube, Facebook and Bluesky, and fills in the schedulers of X, TikTok, LinkedIn, Google Maps and LINE in your own Chrome. **Download** · Quick start · Connect your AI agent · User guide · Support Lazycow · 日本語 You watch the reel, press Approve, and it is booked on the posting calendar *Review, Approve, booked. ▶ **Watch the 40-second demo**: a folder of café clips becomes reels, a person approves one, and it lands on the posting calendar.* ### Connect your AI agent Start the studio first. Then, in Claude Code: ``` claude mcp add lazycow -- npx -y lazycow mcp ``` In Cursor (`.cursor/mcp.json`) or Claude Desktop (`claude_desktop_config.json`): ```json { "mcpServers": { "lazycow": { "command": "npx", "args": ["-y", "lazycow", "mcp"] } } } ``` Claude Code asks "what is waiting for my review?"; the lazycow MCP server lists five reels and says approving stays with you This needs Node 20 or newer on your PATH. The double-click setup keeps its own Node out of your PATH, so use the lines in the studio's **Settings › Keys & AI › Use with Claude or Cursor** instead: they have your paths filled in. The agent can check the studio, make reels, plan posts and publish approved reels. It has no approve tool. Every tool: docs/mcp.md. ## Contents - Connect your AI agent - Quick start - The building blocks - How it works - A person approves every post - Everything stays on your computer - What you need - More, when you need it: first run, a made-up brand, costs, accounts, YouTube, a second studio, AI agents - Documentation - Licence, credit and support ## Quick start ### The easy way: download, unzip, double-click No terminal, no Node, no Python to install first. Just like 1997, minus the CD. 1. Download **Lazycow-Studio-.zip** from the latest release and unzip it somewhere you will keep it. 2. Open **README.TXT** first. Yes, really. It has the steps, and some jokes. 3. Double-click **Start Lazycow** (Mac: right-click **Start Lazycow.command** › Open, the first time). If Windows says "Windows protected your PC", choose **More info › Run anyway**: the file is new, not bad. You can read every line in `scripts/bootstrap/windows.ps1`. 4. A blue 1997-style setup screen asks where to keep the studio's work and where your footage is, then downloads pinned copies of Node, Python and ffmpeg (each checked against its SHA-256, kept in your user folder, no admin rights). It takes 10 to 30 minutes, about 1.5 GB. 5. The studio opens, and Lazy Kenji shows you around. Next time, double-click **Lazycow Studio** on your desktop. Windows 10/11 (64-bit), or a Mac with Apple silicon and macOS 14+. If anything goes wrong, double-click Start Lazycow again: it carries on where it stopped, and `setup.log` says what happened. How it works: scripts/bootstrap/README.md. ### For developers: the terminal way You need Node 20+, Python 3.12+ and a current ffmpeg (details). 1. Get the code: ``` git clone https://github.com/kensaurus/lazycow-studio.git cd lazycow-studio npm ci ``` 2. Set up this computer. This writes `.env`, makes the Python environment, and fetches the picture-quality model and some free music: ``` npm run setup ``` 3. Start the studio: ``` npm run review ``` 4. Open **http://127.0.0.1:4317**. The first load takes 10 to 20 seconds while the search model starts. Follow the **Getting started** list on the page. `npm run setup` ends with a list of anything still missing and the exact fix. Usually that is ffmpeg: put a current `ffmpeg` and `ffprobe` in the data folder's `bin`, or on your PATH. Run it again any time. `npm run setup -- --check` only reports. To choose where things go on a first run: ``` npm run setup -- --data D:\studio-data --footage "D:\My Footage" ``` Both are optional. By default everything the studio makes goes in `./data` beside the code. Your footage is never moved or changed. ## The building blocks | Building block | In plain words | You use it by… | |:--|:--|:--| | **Project** | One brand, client or trip, with its own footage, words, accounts and reels | pressing the project name beside the logo, then **New project** | | **Footage** | Your photos and videos. The studio reads them and never changes them. | **Footage › Add a folder**, or **Add from Google Photos** | | **Theme** | The story of a reel: a headline, two or three true lines, and the kind of shots each line needs | **Reels › Make reels › New theme** | | **Reel** | One short vertical video (9:16), with files cut for each network | **Make reels**, then **Review** | | **Reel style** | The type pairing, colours, how the words arrive, and the colour grade. Each new reel draws its own. | the reel editor's **Type, colours and motion**, or **Surprise me** | | **Approve** | Your yes. Only approved reels are booked or posted. | **Approve** in the editor, after you watch the reel | | **Booking** | A post held for a set time, on the network or by the studio | **Posting › Plan posts**, or **Runs by itself** | | **Version** | A better cut of a reel that is already booked, made beside the live one | **Posting › Versions › Use the new version** or **Keep the live one** | | **Swap** | The studio replaces an older booking with the newest approved render, at the same time slot | **Swap them by themselves** on the Posting page | | **Long video** | A 5 to 15 minute (10 by default), 16:9 YouTube video from a trip, in parts with chapters | **Reels › Long videos** | | **Chrome link** | The studio fills in the X, TikTok, Google Maps, LINE and LinkedIn schedulers in your own signed-in Chrome | **Settings › Keys & AI › Chrome link** (how) | | **MCP** | A way for an AI agent (Claude Code, Claude Desktop, Cursor) to use the studio. It cannot approve. | `claude mcp add lazycow -- npx -y lazycow mcp` (how) | ## How it works | | | |:--|:--| | A folder of café clips in the studio's Footage page **1. A folder of footage.** Point the studio at it. It only reads the files, tags them on your computer and finds them by words. | The Make reels panel: pick themes, then make them **2. Make reels.** Pick a theme or two. Each reel gets clips that fit its words, licence-clean music and every size the networks want. | | The review editor: the reel, its timeline of text, clips, music and effects **3. You review.** Watch it, trim it, swap a clip, change the words. The timeline shows every clip, caption, sound and effect. | Approve on a reel **4. You approve.** Nothing goes anywhere before this. Faces need Consent OK first. | | The posting calendar with the booked posts of the month **5. Booked.** One post a day per network at the hour your audience is awake. Results come back a few days later. | Lazy Kenji's 1997-style pop-up tour **6. Help when you want it.** A guided tour, the Getting started list, Ctrl K to find anything, and a Problems list that says what went wrong. | ```mermaid flowchart LR F[(Your footage
read only)] --> T[Tag and search
on this computer] T --> M[Make reels
theme, approved words,
a style of its own] M --> R{A person
reviews} R -- Reject or edit --> M R -- Approve --> B[Book
one post a day
per network] B --> P[Posted
YouTube, Facebook, Bluesky,
X, TikTok, LINE ...] B -. a better cut is made .-> V{Versions:
a person picks} V -- Use the new version --> S[Swap the bookings
same time slot] S --> P T --> L[Long videos
a trip in 16:9 parts] L --> Y[YouTube
private, unlisted, public
or on a schedule] ``` The Reels page: reels waiting for review, each with its first frame and its words Three programs run on one computer: a Node server and the studio page (`server/`), a Python pipeline (`py/studio/`), and Remotion for the words on screen (`src/`). More in docs/architecture.md. ## A person approves every post This is the one rule the studio never breaks. - A new reel is a draft. It cannot be booked, uploaded or posted until a person presses **Approve**. - A reel with a face in it cannot be approved until someone confirms the person agreed (**Consent OK**), or blurs the face. - When a reel's words change, it goes back to review. - A new version replaces a booked reel only when a person presses **Use the new version**. - AI tools, agents and scripts can make drafts and suggest changes. They cannot approve. ## Everything stays on your computer - Your footage is only read, never changed, and never uploaded to be tagged. Search and tagging run on your own processor (OpenCLIP). - Keys and sign-ins stay in `.env` and in your data folder. They are never in git. - The studio listens on `127.0.0.1` only. Nothing leaves your computer unless you connect a service: a network you post to, or a paid AI tool you add a key for. - On a shared computer, set `STUDIO_API_TOKEN` so other programs need a token. ## What you need | | Minimum (works, slowly) | Recommended | |:--|:--|:--| | Processor | 4 threads | 8 threads or more | | Memory | 6 GB | 12 GB or more | | Free disk for renders | 3 GB | 20 GB or more | | Screen | 1280 px wide | 1440 px or more | Software: **Node 20** or newer, **Python 3.12** or newer, and a current **ffmpeg** (the build must support `-fps_mode`; builds from 2021 do not). A current Chrome, Edge or Safari for the studio page. Windows is where the studio is used every day. macOS and Linux work for the main flow but are tested less. A 9-clip reel takes about 6 to 7 minutes on a 32-thread desktop, and roughly twice that on 8 threads. Press **System** in the top bar to see what your computer can do. ## More, when you need it First run, in order 1. **System** (top bar): every line green or amber. A red line says what is missing. 2. **Footage › Add a folder**: pick your footage. Tagging starts by itself. 3. **Settings › Keys & AI › This project**: your name, link, hashtags, and words the studio must never use. 4. **Reels › Make reels › New theme**: a headline, two or three true lines, and the kind of shots each line needs. 5. **Make reels**, then **Review** each one: watch, trim, swap clips, then **Approve** or **Reject**. 6. **Settings › Accounts**: connect each network once. **Posting › Plan posts** books approved reels, one a day per network. The step-by-step guide is docs/user-guide.md. Try it with a made-up brand Copy the four files in `examples/cafe-kumo/` (`brand.json`, `themes.json`, `words.json`, `profiles.json`) into your data folder before the first `npm run review`. The studio opens as "Cafe Kumo", with two themes and a word bank. Change them in **Settings › Keys & AI › This project** when you start your own. What costs money Nothing, unless you choose it. The studio, its search model, the music and the posting are free. | Optional service | What it adds | Needs | |:--|:--|:--| | fal.ai | Slow motion, sharpening, music made for a reel, a Japanese voice, a "living photo", sound effects, the music bed of a long video | Your key | | OpenRouter | An AI reviewer that suggests fixes and judges a new version, suggested new lines for the word bank, post angles | Your key | | Together AI | Same kinds of tools, as an alternative | Your key | | Firecrawl | **Research** (Posting › Research): reads the web for trends and events nearby (read-only) | Your key | - Every paid call is priced first and refused over your limits: by default 2 USD a day, 2 USD a reel and 20 USD in total. Change them in **Settings › Keys & AI**. - AI never changes an approved reel. It makes a new draft, which a person reviews again. - AI suggestions are suggestions. New words are used only after a person presses **Use it**. - Free music comes from Openverse (CC0 and public domain only, 200 searches a day, no key). Connect your accounts | Network | How the studio posts | You need | |:--|:--|:--| | YouTube Shorts | Uploads as private; YouTube publishes at the time | Your own Google Cloud app (about 10 minutes; the studio walks you through it) | | Facebook Page | Schedules a Page Reel through Meta's API | Your own Meta app's ID and secret | | Bluesky | Sends it at the time (this computer must be on) | Sign in with Bluesky | | X, TikTok, Google Maps, LINE, LinkedIn | Fills in each site's own scheduler in your Chrome | The Chrome link (docs/helper.md) and you signed in there | | Instagram, others | You post by hand from the approved folder | Nothing | - The studio posts only to accounts you connected, and only approved reels. - Turn each network on or off for a project in **Settings › Accounts**. A new project starts with all of them off. - Posts the studio sends itself (Bluesky, and posts marked "the studio sends it") go out for every project, whichever project is open. Leave the computer on at those times. - **YouTube's upload allowance.** Since 1 June 2026, YouTube gives each Google Cloud app its own allowance of 100 uploads a day (YouTube Data API). The automatic swap uses at most 20 of them a day. The rest are for new posts and long videos. Details: docs/integrations.md. Several YouTube accounts, and long videos on YouTube A project can connect more than one YouTube channel. - **main** is the channel your Shorts post to. - **a2, a3, ...** are more channels: a personal channel for long videos, or a second brand. Each has its own sign-in. - Connect them in **Settings › Keys & AI**, in the box **YouTube: Google account and app**: press **Connect another account**. They are listed there under **Other YouTube accounts**. - One Google app can serve every project. Press **Use this Google app in every project** in the same box. A project made in the studio can then connect its own channels without an app of its own. Long videos upload from **Reels › Long videos**. Pick the account and who can see them: | Choice | What happens | |:--|:--| | Private | Only you see it in YouTube Studio | | Unlisted | Only people with the link can watch | | Public | On the channel and in search at once | | Go public on a schedule | Private until each part's time, then public. The first part goes at the time you pick, then one every N days. | The title, the description with chapters, the tags and the thumbnail go with it. The link shows on the part when it is up. From a terminal in the `py` folder, with the studio's Python (the venv in your data folder): ``` python -m studio youtube accounts python -m studio youtube upload-vlog --part 1 --account a2 --privacy unlisted python -m studio youtube upload-vlog --part 2 --account a2 --at 2026-12-01T19:00 ``` `--at` is this computer's local time. The part stays private until then. A second studio for another project Work on a second project without switching the main studio away. Start a second studio pinned to that project, on its own port: ``` STUDIO_PROJECT=my-trip STUDIO_PORT=4318 STUDIO_QUIET=1 npm run review ``` On Windows (cmd), set each variable first: `set STUDIO_PROJECT=my-trip`, `set STUDIO_PORT=4318`, `set STUDIO_QUIET=1`. Then run `npm run review`. - `STUDIO_PROJECT` is the project's id (its folder name under `~/.lazycow/projects`). The pinned studio never switches project. - `STUDIO_QUIET=1` makes it a studio for looking and editing only. It does not post, book, swap or check by itself. The main studio still sends due posts for every project. - Connect YouTube in the main studio on port 4317 (see the note in `.env.example`). Use it from Claude Code, Claude Desktop or Cursor (MCP) The studio has an MCP server. An AI agent can check the studio, make reels, watch renders, plan posts and publish **approved** reels. It has no approve tool. ``` npm run review claude mcp add lazycow -- npx -y lazycow mcp ``` From a clone, without npm: `claude mcp add lazycow -- node C:\path\to\lazycow-studio\server\mcp.mjs`. **Settings › Keys & AI › Use with Claude or Cursor** shows these lines with your paths filled in. Full guide: docs/mcp.md. ## Documentation | Read | When you want to | |:--|:--| | User guide | use the studio page by page, or fix a problem | | Architecture | know how the pieces fit, and where data lives | | MCP | let an AI agent use the studio | | Chrome link | schedule X, TikTok, Google Maps, LINE and LinkedIn | | Connected services | see each outside service and why it is used | | AI tools, results, research | call those parts of the HTTP API | | HTTP API | see every route (OpenAPI 3.1) | | Roadmap, changes | see what is next and what changed | ## Licence The studio's code is under the **Apache License 2.0**. > **Remotion is not open source in the same way.** The studio uses Remotion to draw the words on screen. Remotion has its own licence: it is free for individuals, non-profits and companies of up to 3 people. **A for-profit company with more than 3 people needs a Remotion company licence to make reels with the studio.** That licence is between you and Remotion; the studio's Apache licence does not cover it. Every other component, model, font and piece of music, with its licence, is listed in THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md. The fonts in `public/fonts` each have their licence file beside them. Each reel's music credit travels with it in `credits.txt`. The names "Lazycow" and "Lazycow Studio" and the icon are trademarks of kensaurus LLC and are not covered by the licence. A fork needs its own name and icon: see TRADEMARKS.md. ## Credit and contributing Lazycow Studio is made by **Kenji Sakuramoto (kensaurus)** and contributors, and published by kensaurus LLC. - **Using it?** Nothing to do. A link back to https://kensaur.us is always appreciated. - **Forking it?** Keep `LICENSE` and `NOTICE`, give your fork its own name and icon, and please keep "Based on Lazycow Studio by kensaurus" in your About screen. - **Helping?** Read CONTRIBUTING.md and the Code of Conduct. Security problems: SECURITY.md. - **Writing about it?** Use "Cite this repository" on GitHub (CITATION.cff). ## Support Lazycow The studio is free and stays free. If it saves you evenings of editing, you can pay for its development: once, any amount, or monthly with small benefits (your requests looked at first, your name or logo in the About window). | | | |:--|:--| | **Pay once** | In yen · In US dollars | | **Monthly** | Supporter ¥500 / $4 · Backer ¥1,500 / $10 · Sponsor ¥5,000 / $35 | What each plan includes, and how to cancel: SUPPORTING.md. Thank you to everyone who does. # ericwang915/agent-hive

body:
# ericwang915/agent-hive

🐝 One Queen, many bees: an open-source Mac app that turns Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI and Cursor Agent into a hive. Schedules, event triggers, squads with review loops, a honeycomb view. No API keys.

## Languages

- Shell

- agent-manager
- agent-orchestration
- agentic-coding
- ai-agents
- ai-coding

## Top Contributors

---

## README

 
 Agent Hive 
 One Queen. Many bees. Your coding agents, working as a hive. 
A free, open-source Mac app that turns Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI and Cursor Agent into a team you can watch, schedule and steer. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Install · Features · How it compares · FAQ 
 

Agent Hive running a relay team of coding agents: one bee writes, another reviews and sends it back, a third tests

## What is Agent Hive?

Agent Hive is a macOS app that runs several coding-agent CLIs at once and lets them work as a team. Each agent is a **bee**: Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, Cursor Agent, or any command you like, working in its own folder. You can talk to each bee, put it on a schedule, chain bees into a relay where one writes and another reviews, or pull them into a group and let **Queen** hand out the work.

It uses the CLIs and logins you already have, including a Claude or ChatGPT subscription. It ships no API keys, stores none, has no account and no server of its own.

## Highlights

- **Any agent, mixed in one team.** Claude Code writes, Codex reviews, Gemini tests. Any CLI that takes a prompt can be a bee.
- **Agents that work while you are away.** Schedules (once, daily, weekdays, weekends, weekly, monthly, every N minutes) and event triggers (new commits, GitHub pull requests, comments and CI failures, another bee finishing), catch-up for runs missed while the Mac slept, and a daily budget that stops automatic runs when it is used up.
- **A lead agent instead of ten terminals.** Tell Queen what you want; she picks the bees, dispatches the work, waits for the results and sums them up.
- **Everything they made, in one place.** A Files page lists every PDF, deck, chart and link the bees produced, by bee and project. Search finds bees, skills, memory and anything said in a conversation.
- **Review built into the flow.** Relay teams send a reviewer's findings back to the writer until it approves. Every bee has a diff view with commit, push and pull request.
- **Spends fewer tokens than the CLI on its own.** Sessions are compacted before they get expensive, scheduled runs start fresh, unused tools and MCP servers are left out. In a measured three-round task a bee carried about 30% less context per round than plain `claude -p` on the same machine with the same setup (29k against 44k tokens).
- **It remembers.** Overnight, two helper bees turn the day's conversations into long-term memory and reusable skills. New sessions start with both.
- **Nothing to trust but your own machine.** MIT licensed, no build step, no telemetry; the only request the app makes on its own is a check for new releases on GitHub. The app is signed and notarized by Apple and updates itself if you let it.

## Install

```bash
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ericwang915/agent-hive/main/install.sh | bash
```

This downloads the latest release for your Mac (Apple silicon or Intel), puts `Agent Hive.app` in `/Applications` and opens it. You can also download the `.dmg` from the releases page. The app is signed and notarized by Apple.

To run from source instead:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/ericwang915/agent-hive.git
cd agent-hive
npm install
npm start
```

### Requirements

- macOS 12 or later
- At least one agent CLI on your `PATH`: `claude`, `codex`, `gemini` or `cursor-agent`. Queen, the daily report and the night bees need `claude`.
- `git` for diffs, commits, branches and pull requests. `gh` is optional and used to open pull requests.

## What you can do with it

### Let Queen lead a group

Pull bees into a group and tell Queen what you want. She picks the right bees, dispatches the work, waits for the results and sums them up. She only wakes the bees she needs, and she asks before hatching new ones.

Queen dispatches two bees and reports back

A group works without Queen too. `@mention` a bee and it starts right away. Leave the name out and a small, cheap model picks the bee the message is for, so the others stay asleep; a bee with nothing to add stays quiet. Stickers work both ways. A bee can hand part of the job to another by `@mentioning` it, for at most three hops.

### Chain bees into a relay team

Up to four bees share a folder and pass work down the line. A reviewer can send its findings back to the writer until it approves, for at most three rounds. Bees on the same step run in parallel, each in its own git worktree, and a final bee merges their results. The clip at the top is one such team.

A relay team is also a **squad** with a name. Queen can hand it a whole job with one call and hears back once, when the chain is finished or stuck. You can start it yourself from any group: `@Shop-squad add an export button`. The group shows the chain and each bee's state as it runs.

### Read every step, then review the diff

Each bee has its own chat window with the full conversation. Replies stream in as they are written, edits show as inline diffs, sub-agents are nested, and every round shows its cost. Type `@` to point at a file, `/` for commands, Shift-Tab to switch between Ask, Auto-edit and Plan. The bee's folder sits in a sidebar on the left, and file paths in the conversation are clickable: they open at the line mentioned. The Files tab is a small editor: create, rename and delete files and folders, edit and save, find in a file, and search the whole folder by name or text. The Changes tab shows the diff. Commit, discard, push and open a pull request from there, or keep a bee on its own branch and merge when you are happy.

A bee's chat, then its diff

### See the whole hive at a glance

The Hive page opens as a honeycomb; a switch takes you to the classic cards. Each squad is a cluster shaped by its relay: a chain sits in a row, a review loop is marked on the shared edge, and bees that work in parallel fan out and meet again at the merge. Click a cell and its full card, with every button, shows beside the comb.

The honeycomb view: a squad with a review loop, a squad with two bees in parallel and a merge, and three bees on their own

### Hatch a bee in a few clicks

Pick a folder, an engine and a model. Give it a prompt and a schedule, or leave both empty and just talk to it.

The hatch dialog

### And the rest

- **Schedules.** Once, daily, weekly, monthly, or every N minutes. Runs missed while the Mac slept are caught up the same day.
- **Event triggers.** Instead of a time, a bee can wait for something to happen: new commits on a branch (in its folder or on the remote), a GitHub event (new pull request, new comment, CI failure, through the `gh` CLI), or another bee finishing or failing. What happened is attached to its prompt. Its own commits and comments do not wake it, and a cooldown keeps bursts to one run.
- **Sleep-safe.** Running bees stop when the lid closes and pick up where they left off when it opens, or when the app restarts.
- **Permissions.** Approve each action from the app (Claude Code), auto-accept edits, allow everything, or plan first and change nothing. Switch at any time from the chat.
- **Context.** A meter shows how full a Claude Code bee's session is. `/compact` summarises it on the spot, and `/new` starts over.
- **Token savers.** A session that is half full (100k tokens at most), or large and idle for an hour, is compacted before its next round. Scheduled runs start a new session. Each bee's settings list your MCP servers, so you tick only the ones it needs. Reports and the night bees use a smaller model. All adjustable.
- **Spend.** Cost and tokens per round, and a daily budget that holds back automatic runs once it is used up.
- **Memory and skills.** Overnight, *Dreamer* tidies long-term memory and *Gardener* turns the day's conversations into reusable skills. New sessions start with both.
- **Dashboard.** A 24-hour activity timeline, spend, and Queen's daily report.
- **Upgrades.** When a newer release is out, an Upgrade button appears in the sidebar. It downloads the release, checks that it is signed by the same developer, swaps the app and restarts. Settings (the gear at the bottom of the sidebar) can install new versions automatically once no bee is working, and notify you when one is out.
- **Ranks.** Every finished round counts. A bee climbs from Bronze through Silver, Gold, Platinum and Diamond to Master, and its look changes with each rank.
- **Files page.** Everything the bees produced in one list, newest first: files they wrote or named in a reply (PDFs, decks, charts, CSVs) and links they gave (artifacts, Google Slides, pull requests). Each row shows the bee and its project; filter by kind or bee, open the file, or jump to it in the bee's window.
- **Chats in the sidebar.** Every bee and squad in one list: its name and what it is for, or what it is doing right now. A squad folds into one line and opens when something is going on.
- **Search everything.** The search box and ⌘K find bees, skills, memory, and what was said in any bee's conversation or group; a hit opens the chat at that message.
- **Right-click anything.** Rename, settings, stop and delete for bees and groups.

## How it compares

Several good tools run coding agents in parallel. They differ in what they are built around. This is how Agent Hive sees the field in November 2026; check each project for its current features.

| Tool | Built around | Good fit when |
|---|---|---|
| **Agent Hive** | A standing team: scheduled agents, a lead agent (Queen), relay teams with review loops, memory and skills. Open source, macOS. | You want agents that keep working on a schedule, hand work to each other, and that you can supervise from one window. |
| Conductor | Parallel workspaces, each agent in its own git worktree. A proprietary macOS app. | You want to start many independent tasks on one repository and review each branch. |
| Claude Squad | A terminal UI on tmux, each agent in its own git worktree. Open source. | You live in the terminal and want sessions that survive a closed window. |
| Vibe Kanban | A kanban board of tasks that agents pick up in workspaces. Open source. | You think in tickets and want a board as the main view. |
| Claude Code agent teams | Several Claude Code instances that message each other. Claude only. | You use only Claude Code and want it to split one task among teammates. |

What Agent Hive adds on top of running agents side by side:

- **Scheduling with catch-up, sleep-safe runs and a daily budget**, so unattended work is predictable.
- **Routing by a small model.** In a group, a message without an `@mention` goes only to the bee it concerns; the others stay asleep and cost nothing.
- **Review loops across engines**: a reviewer on one model can send work back to a writer on another, for at most three rounds.
- **Token controls you can see**: a context meter, automatic compaction, cost per round, and a checklist of MCP servers per bee.
- **Memory and skills** that are distilled from your own conversations and shared by every bee.

Agent Hive also uses git worktrees, for bees that run in parallel on the same step of a relay.

## Safety

Bees run real commands on your machine, with the permission level you choose. "Allow all" skips every confirmation, so only use it in folders you trust.

The app listens on `127.0.0.1` on a random port, protected by a per-launch token. Claude Code uses it to ask for permission decisions, and Queen uses it to call her tools. Nothing is exposed to the network.

State lives in `~/Library/Application Support/Agent Hive/`. Workspaces, skills and memory live under `~/AgentHive/` by default.

## FAQ

### Is Agent Hive free?

Yes. It is open source under the MIT license. You pay only for the agent CLIs you already use, through their own subscriptions or API billing.

### Does it need an API key?

No. Agent Hive starts the CLIs installed on your Mac (`claude`, `codex`, `gemini`, `cursor-agent`) with the logins they already have. It never sees or stores a key.

### Does it work with a Claude Pro or Max subscription, or ChatGPT Plus?

Yes. If the CLI works in your terminal, it works as a bee, with the same account and limits.

### Which coding agents does it support?

Claude Code, Codex CLI, Gemini CLI and Cursor Agent out of the box, plus any command line that accepts a prompt (a custom template with `{prompt}`). Queen, the daily report and the night bees need Claude Code.

### How is it different from Claude Code subagents or agent teams?

Subagents and agent teams are features of Claude Code and use Claude only. Agent Hive runs separate, long-lived agents from different vendors, each with its own folder, session, schedule and chat window, and keeps running them after you close the conversation.

### Can agents run on a schedule, like a cron job for Claude Code?

Yes. Each bee can run once, daily, weekly, monthly or every N minutes. Runs missed while the Mac slept are caught up the same day, and a daily budget can stop automatic runs.

### Does my code leave my machine?

Agent Hive has no server and sends your code nowhere. The agent CLIs talk to their own providers exactly as they do in your terminal. The only request the app makes on its own is a check for new releases on GitHub.

### Does it run on Windows or Linux?

Not yet. It is built and tested for macOS 12 or later, on Apple silicon and Intel.

### How do I update it?

An Upgrade button appears in the sidebar when a new release is out. Settings can also install new versions automatically once no bee is working.

## How it is built

No build step and no framework: plain HTML, CSS and JS in the renderer, Electron in the main process, two small dependencies for Markdown.

| File | Role |
|---|---|
| `main.js` | Main process: state, process management, scheduling, relay execution, git, approvals, groups and Queen |
| `core.js` | Engines and command lines, schedule keys, output parsers, relay planning, git and worktree helpers |
| `team.js` | Relay-team graph helpers, shared by main and renderer |
| `queen.js` | Queen's tools, dispatch rules and result parsing |
| `garden.js` | Skills and memory files, Dreamer and Gardener prompts |
| `events.js` | Event triggers: checking the settings, telling what is new on GitHub, matching a finished bee |
| `outputs.js` | Files page: finding the files and links a bee produced in its log |
| `update.js` | Upgrade: finding, downloading, verifying and installing a newer release |
| `files.js` | File browser: listing, reading and locating paths inside a bee's folder |
| `approve-mcp.js`, `hive-mcp.js` | Small MCP stdio servers that call back into the app |
| `index.html`, `app.js` | Main window |
| `chat.html`, `chat.js` | Per-bee chat window |
| `test.js` | Unit tests for everything that does not need Electron |

```bash
npm test             # unit tests
npm run dist         # build an ad-hoc signed .zip and .dmg into dist/
npm run dist:signed  # the same, signed and notarized (needs CSC_NAME and NOTARYTOOL_PROFILE)
```

## Contributing

Issues and pull requests are welcome. See CONTRIBUTING.md for how the code is laid out and how to add an engine.

- Default branch: main

## Languages

- Astro
- CSS

- Go
- HTML
- JavaScript
- Just
- MDX
- Shell
- TypeScript

## Topics

- ai-agent
- apm

- monitoring

## Top Contributors

## README

# Pitot

Pitot (pronounced **PEE-toh**).

**Observability your agents can operate.** Send OpenTelemetry to one binary, then investigate with
Pitot's built-in agent or connect your own over MCP.

CI
License: Apache 2.0
Go Reference

 
 
 
 
 
 

*Current Pitot interface with deterministic offline sample telemetry.*

Pitot keeps OpenTelemetry traces, logs, and metrics in one binary and one data directory, with no
external storage services to operate. Pitot is pre-release and changes without migration paths; the browser
client, built-in agent, MCP tools, dashboards, and alerts are preview capabilities
(status). Start with the
documentation or run it below.

- OTLP ingest over gRPC and HTTP, with local Parquet storage and DuckDB analytics.
- Explore and PitotQL for querying telemetry without an AI provider.
- An investigation agent that answers questions about your telemetry in plain language.
- An MCP server for external agents using the same typed query tools.
- Dashboards across traces, logs, and metrics, and alerts on service error rate, latency,
 throughput, and log volume.

## Quick start

### Docker

```sh
docker run --name pitot --restart unless-stopped -p 7520:7520 \
  -v pitot-data:/var/lib/pitot/data \
  -e PITOT_AUTH_CODE_SECRET=$(openssl rand -hex 32) \
  labstack/pitot:latest
```

Open the one-time setup URL printed by the container and create the first administrator. Pitot
displays the ingest token exactly once, unless `PITOT_INGEST_TOKEN` already set it; save it with your collector secrets. For later sign-in
without SMTP, mint a 15-minute, single-use link against the running container's control database:

```sh
docker exec pitot pitot login-link admin@example.com
```

The UI, API, MCP, and both OTLP transports share port `7520`. See
installation for image defaults and bind-mount ownership, and
first boot for setup and SMTP login.

### Native binary

Install a checksum-verified release for Linux or macOS, amd64 or arm64:

```sh
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/labstack/pitot/main/scripts/install.sh | sh
export PITOT_AUTH_CODE_SECRET=$(openssl rand -hex 32)
pitot
```

Set `PITOT_VERSION` to a release tag, such as `v2026.11.0-alpha`, to pin a release, and `PITOT_PREFIX` to choose the installation
directory. Native installs bind `127.0.0.1:7520`; set `PITOT_ADDR=:7520` for remote access, then
follow the same first-boot setup.

### Send telemetry

A standard OTLP/HTTP exporter can use the saved ingest token:

```sh
export OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_PROTOCOL=http/protobuf
export OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT=http://localhost:7520
export OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_HEADERS="authorization=Bearer%20$INGEST_TOKEN"
```

For a Collector on the same private container network, the forwarding side is:

```yaml
exporters:
  otlp_http/pitot:
    endpoint: http://pitot:7520
    headers:
      Authorization: "Bearer ${env:INGEST_TOKEN}"

service:
  pipelines:
    traces:  { receivers: [otlp], exporters: [otlp_http/pitot] }
    metrics: { receivers: [otlp], exporters: [otlp_http/pitot] }
    logs:    { receivers: [otlp], exporters: [otlp_http/pitot] }
```

Use an existing `otlp` receiver, set `INGEST_TOKEN`, and replace `pitot` with the Collector's
reachable private hostname. OTLP/gRPC uses `localhost:7520` locally; see send
telemetry for TLS and HTTP/2 setup.

### Enable chat

Select `PITOT_AI_PROVIDER=anthropic` and inject `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, or select
`PITOT_AI_PROVIDER=openai` and inject `OPENAI_API_KEY`, then restart Pitot; the selected provider
requires its key at startup. With no provider, chat is disabled and the other features still work.
See AI settings.

### Connect an MCP client

Set `PITOT_PUBLIC_URL` to your stable, externally reachable HTTPS origin, then point a remote MCP
client at that origin's `/mcp` endpoint. The client discovers and registers through OAuth; you
authorize its scopes in the browser. Pitot serves MCP `2026-07-28` and, through the `initialize`
handshake, `2025-11-25` and `2025-06-18` over Streamable HTTP. See connect over
MCP for setup and permissions.

## How it compares

| If you use | Where Pitot differs |
| --- | --- |
| **Grafana with Loki, Tempo, and Mimir** | That stack keeps a service and a query language per signal, plus object storage underneath. Pitot keeps one process, one data directory, and one typed contract across all three signals, at the cost of the horizontal scale those components are built for. |
| **SigNoz** | Both are OTLP-native and self-hosted. SigNoz composes a collector, ClickHouse, and query services; Pitot compiles ingest, authoritative Parquet storage, indexed trace reads, DuckDB analytics, alerting, and the browser client into one binary. |
| **Jaeger** | Jaeger covers traces and expects a storage backend you run separately. Pitot ingests traces, logs, and metrics into the same store, with nothing else to deploy. |
| **Prometheus with Grafana** | Prometheus pulls metrics and is excellent at them. Pitot accepts pushed OTLP for all three signals and is built around investigating a specific incident rather than maintaining long-range metric series. |
| **Datadog**, **Honeycomb**, **Grafana Cloud** | Those are managed services: someone else runs the storage, the scaling, and the upgrades, and your telemetry leaves your network to get there. Pitot is a binary you run, on data that stays on your disk. |
| **An OpenTelemetry Collector piped into ClickHouse** | The same shape, assembled by hand: collector, database, dashboards, and the glue between them. Pitot is that assembly as one program, with an agent and an MCP server already wired to the same query contract. |

Pitot is a single node. It has no clustering, no replication, and no object tier; a deployment that
outgrows one machine's disk and CPU has outgrown Pitot.

## Architecture

One process contains ingest, storage, query, alerts, the agent, MCP, and the React client. Browser
and agent clients share a typed observability contract.

Pitot runtime architecture: OTLP ingest and commit workers publish Parquet; the browser API, agent runtime, and MCP server share queries and dashboards, with DuckDB query state, SQLite control state, anomaly detection, and webhook alerts.

Parquet holds telemetry, DuckDB query state is rebuildable, and SQLite holds transactional product
state. See how storage works for durable ingest,
indexed reads, and compaction while reads continue.

Telemetry durability and query flow: authenticated OTLP rows pass through group admission, parallel commit workers, and durable publication into immutable Parquet batches; indexed trace reads, DuckDB SQL, retention, and compaction use those batches, while service and edge rollups populate rebuildable query state.

## Configuration

Configuration is environment-only: built-in defaults followed by nonempty process environment
values, validated before data files or listeners open. Settings are read once at startup; every
change requires a restart.

| Environment variable | Default | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `PITOT_ADDR` | `127.0.0.1:7520` | UI, API, MCP, and both OTLP transports |
| `PITOT_DATA_DIR` | `./data` | Parquet, query state, and control SQLite |
| `PITOT_AUTH_MODE` | `local` | Login link or SMTP, or `oidc` |
| `PITOT_AUTH_CODE_SECRET` | — | Required in local mode and for OIDC break-glass links, 32+ characters |
| `PITOT_AI_PROVIDER` | — | Empty disables chat; `anthropic` or `openai` enables it |
| `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` | — | Required for Anthropic chat |
| `OPENAI_API_KEY` | — | Required for OpenAI chat |
| `PITOT_RETENTION_DAYS` | `30` | Telemetry retention window |
| `PITOT_MCP_ENABLED` | `true` | Serve the MCP endpoint at `/mcp` |

Every secret accepts ` _FILE` instead of its value; see the settings
reference for validation and runtime secret
delivery for deployment examples.

### Advanced DuckDB sizing

Pitot sizes DuckDB automatically; measured workloads can override memory, connections, and threads
as described in DuckDB sizing.

For TLS, health checks, backups, upgrades, retention, and recovery, see the operator
runbook.

## Performance

Pitot v2026.11.0-alpha accepted **507,311 mixed OpenTelemetry items/s**
over 306.8 seconds on a Hetzner Cloud ccx33 (8 dedicated vCPUs, 32 GB RAM), with
telemetrygen on a separate ccx33. The ingest run on 6 November 2026 passed every
quality gate. See the performance methodology.
Pitot Bench reproduces the measurement on your hardware.

## Build from source

- **Go 1.27.3 and a C/C++ toolchain** on native Linux or macOS, amd64 or arm64.
 Build with `just build` or `bash scripts/with-duckdb.sh go build ./cmd/pitot`;
 the wrapper supplies DuckDB's pinned headers, static libraries, and CGO flags.
 The first build needs network access to download the checksum-verified engine.
- **Bun** — compiles the browser assets
- **Node.js 24.19.0** — runs development helpers and builds the documentation site
- **just** — task runner
- A 32-character **authentication code secret**

```sh
git clone https://github.com/labstack/pitot.git
cd pitot
just install   # browser dependencies and git hooks
just build     # browser assets, then the binary
```

Run it with the minimum configuration:

```sh
export PITOT_AUTH_CODE_SECRET=$(openssl rand -hex 32) # must be 32+ characters

./bin/pitot
```

Open and follow first-boot setup. SMTP and chat are optional; without SMTP,
run `./bin/pitot login-link admin@example.com` with the same configuration and data directory.

## Development

Run `just` to list recipes, `just check` for the full gate, `just test` for Go tests, and `just ui`
to rebuild embedded browser assets. See CONTRIBUTING.md for environment setup,
generated assets, hooks, and project layout.

## Releases

Versions are CalVer — `vYYYY.M.N[-alpha|-beta|-rc]`, numbered from 0 within each month across all
maturity suffixes. Pitot is alpha (for example, `v2026.11.0-alpha`); GA has no suffix.
Container tags omit the leading `v`, and every release moves `latest`. Tagged releases publish
identical manifests to Docker Hub (`labstack/pitot`) and GHCR (`ghcr.io/labstack/pitot`); GHCR is
canonical and also carries development images.

| Image tag | Points at |
| --- | --- |
| `labstack/pitot:latest` | the newest release, mirrored on Docker Hub |
| `labstack/pitot:2026.11.0-alpha` | that exact release, mirrored on Docker Hub |
| `ghcr.io/labstack/pitot:latest` | the newest release |
| `ghcr.io/labstack/pitot:2026.11.0-alpha` | that exact release |
| `ghcr.io/labstack/pitot:main` | the tip of `main` |
| `ghcr.io/labstack/pitot:sha- ` | one specific commit |

See docs/release.md for platforms, checksums, provenance, and verification.

## Contributing

Issues and pull requests are welcome; follow CONTRIBUTING.md and run `just check`
and `just test-race` before opening a pull request. Report security issues through
SECURITY.md.

## Scope

This repository builds Pitot without another repository; LabStack's deployment configuration,
uptime monitoring, and public demo instance are not included. The documentation site in
`site/` is included, with settings pages generated from the same `internal/config` type the
loader binds and checked by `just check`.

## License

Apache-2.0 © LabStack LLC. See NOTICE and
THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES for attribution, and
TRADEMARK for use of the Pitot name and logo.

title: Show HN: Solve hard jigsaw puzzles scanning with phone
author: javierluraschi
body:
Puzzle Solver 
How it works 
 What to expect 
 FAQ 
A jigsaw puzzle solver for the hard ones
That piece fits somewhere. Your phone knows where . 
Scan your pieces one at a time on a printed card. Puzzle Solver traces each outline to a fraction of a millimetre, reads all four sides, and works out which pieces lock together. It's built for the hard ones: endless sky, swirling paint, hundreds of pieces that all look alike.
Sign in to start a puzzle 
 Try the demo: 54 real pieces 
No app to install. Your photos never leave your phone. Open source on GitHub . Or start without an account (it stays in this browser only).
Welcome back . What are we solving today?
Start a puzzle 
or open a demo catalog of 54 real pieces → 
The Starry Night , Vincent van Gogh, 1889: widely considered one of the hardest jigsaw puzzles you can attempt. Shown on the outlines of 54 real pieces from our demo, placed where the solver put them. 
Your puzzles
1 printed card, used for every piece 
1 piece at a time, numbered as you go 
<1 mm outline detail, traced on your phone 
0 photos uploaded: only the outline is saved 
How it works
Four steps, from pile to picture 
No dumping the box on a scanner, no magic photo of the whole pile. You scan each piece on its own, so the app can measure it properly. It sounds slow, but it's what makes the matches trustworthy.
01 
 Print the scan card
Before your first scan, print our scan card page . It's one sheet with four 70 mm cards, each with a thick black frame. That frame is the scanner's ruler: it tells the app exactly how big each piece is and straightens out the camera angle, so every outline comes out true to size.
Print at 100% / actual size . A 50 mm check line on the sheet lets you confirm it.
Start with the magenta card ; after each scan the app tells you if another card shows that piece more clearly.
The card is required. The scanner waits until it sees the frame.
🖨 Open the printable card 
02 
 Scan one piece at a time
Put one piece face up in the middle of the card and hold your phone flat above it. A level shows how you're tilted. When the frame turns green and you hold still, the photo takes itself. The light switches on automatically where your phone allows it.
The outline is traced right on your phone at full camera resolution, with shadows filtered out. You get a preview to check before you move on.
Hold it flat , within 3°: the dot has to sit inside the small circle.
Get close , so the card fills the view. The app tells you if you're too far.
Prefer your camera app? Tap 🖼 to shoot at full resolution with flash.
03 
 Number it, keep it
Each scan gets the next number: 1, 2, 3… Pencil it lightly on the back of the piece, or set the piece on a numbered sticky note or in an egg-carton slot. Later, when the app says " 42 goes just left of 28 " , you'll know exactly which piece to grab.
Every piece is saved the moment you scan it , so you can stop and pick up later.
Typo? Labels can be edited, and a bad scan can be redone.
04 
 Match and solve
Open any piece to see its best partners for each side, ranked by how snugly they fit. Or tap Solve and the app assembles your catalog into groups: a map of numbered pieces, each in its place, ready for you to build from.
Every side is sorted as a tab , a blank or a flat edge , so corners and border pieces are found for you.
Scan on your phone, then open the solution on a bigger screen. With an account, your puzzles follow you.
What to expect
Honest expectations 
Scanning is the slow part
It becomes a rhythm: place, hold, check, number, next. Budget an evening for a few hundred pieces and split big puzzles over several sessions. Solving takes seconds.
You don't have to scan everything
Only scanned pieces can be matched, so scan the part you're stuck on: all the sky, the border, one tricky colour. A few dozen pieces from the same area is plenty to start.
Shape is everything
Matching reads only the outline, never the picture. The swirls that make The Starry Night so hard by eye don't confuse it, and neither does a plain sky. It works best with grid-cut puzzles whose pieces differ in shape (Ravensburger-style). Cuts where many pieces look identical are harder.
Groups, not guesses
The solver is careful. It only joins pieces when every touching side agrees, so expect several solid groups rather than one risky answer. On a 500-piece reference set it put 489 pieces in one group, with 99.8% of neighbours right.
Your photos stay on your phone
The image is processed on your device and then thrown away. Only the outline, a list of points, and its number are saved.
Just a browser
Open this page on a recent phone with a camera. There's nothing to install. Allow camera access when asked, and you're scanning.
Under the hood
Why one piece at a time works
With a single piece on a known card, the app can afford to be precise. It corrects perspective with the card's frame and measures in real millimetres. It separates the piece from its shadow by colour rather than brightness, then traces the edge with sub-pixel accuracy.
The four corners split the outline into four sides. Each side is checked against every other side by fitting the two shapes together and measuring what's left over, allowing for the hairline gap real neighbours have. The solver then grows groups from the most certain matches and backs out a piece if its neighbours disagree.
It's all open source, with the details in the GitHub repository .
FAQ
Good questions 
Do I need an account? 
 Not to look around: the demo works without one. Sign in with Cloudish to keep your catalog safe and open it on any device, for example scanning on your phone and browsing the solution on a laptop. You can also start without an account, but then the puzzle is only remembered by that browser.
Do I really have to print the card? 
 Yes. The black frame is how the scanner knows the true size of a piece and corrects for the camera angle. Without it, two photos of the same piece would differ and matching would suffer. One sheet is enough for a whole puzzle; if you don't have a printer, any copy shop or library can print it.
Why one piece at a time instead of a photo of the whole pile? 
 Precision. Matching depends on outlines being right to a fraction of a millimetre. One piece, centred on a known card and photographed flat at full resolution, gets there. A crowded table photo doesn't.
Which puzzles work best? 
 Classic grid-cut puzzles where each piece has four sides with tabs and blanks, and the shapes vary from piece to piece. Puzzles with many identical shapes, or irregular "random cut" pieces, are much harder because shape is all the app looks at. What's hard by eye is fine: night skies, oceans, paintings like The Starry Night . That's where the app helps most.
What if a scan comes out wrong? 
 You see every outline before you move on, so just scan it again. From the catalog you can also re-scan, relabel or delete any piece later.
Are my pictures uploaded anywhere? 
 No. Photos are processed on your phone and then discarded. The server only receives each piece's outline and label, and uses them to compute matches.
Is it open source? 
 Yes, under the MIT license. The scanner, the matcher and the solver are all on GitHub . Stars, issues and pull requests are welcome.
Clear the table. Grab a pencil. Let's find where it goes.

Don't forget to print the scan card first.

Headings are set in Fraunces (OFL). The Starry Night by Vincent van Gogh (1889, Museum of Modern Art) is in the public domain; image via Wikimedia Commons .

comments.text: I got a super hard jigsaw puzzle and got frustrated by it. I tried some of the apps and services out there but nothing worked, mostly cause this puzzle was close to single color so the only way to match the pieces was by shape.This project started with an existing PHP solver (https://github.com/byWulf/jigsawlutioner) but after trying it many things were broken, the phone outlines not accurate enough, I found out direct geometric side matching worked better, so I rewrote it from scratch (with AI obviously) in plain Node with no deps and used the old results just as a reference.Scanning took the most time. Problem was that live segmentation overheated the phone, so I changed it so it only finds the card live and does the outline after the photo.Shadows were bad as well, part—early edges included dark crescents and came out 7-9% too big. So switched to printing a PDF to scan the cards and then also change snapping the edge at full res.Ended up printing a few card colors because some pieces vanish against certain backgrounds, but then found out most reliable to scan the pieces from the back for consistency.Assembly is strongest-first with some local backtracking when groups almost close but conflict.There’s a 54-piece demo that solves cleanly; it also does okay on a 1000-piece set.Still rough on pieces that are close in color to the card, and the gap can be sensitive to how you scan.The “match these three pieces” thing was added later for when you just want the missing corner of a 2x2 ranked. Which was useful cause even this algorithm was not able to match everything.The last few pieces of the puzzle I matched them by hand (so this project won’t match all the pieces) but that was the remaining 10% of the puzzle and was quite fun and enjoyable.Repo: https://github.com/javierluraschi/puzzle

title: Show HN: Archiver – free extract/compaction tool built with WebAssembly
author: nzbman
body: I maintain a handful of archive libraries written in Rust and I had the crazy idea to throw them all together in a browser app, doing intense computational work, fully local in the browser. I've wanted to learn more about WebAssembly and this was a great opportunity to really see what it can do.Nothing is uploaded, there's no server behind it. Everything processes local and it even works offline and on mobile. I made a 7z on my phone in airplane mode today.There's a couple other tools like this out there, but they have sign-ups, ads, limitations. Archiver is a free tool for anyone and the only limits are what your disk can hold.For 7z specifically, it also picks the best compression filters for every file in the archive based on the file type, which is really powerful when you're archiving large, mixed data (text+pictures+binary) folders.Hope you enjoy.

title: Show HN: Ruscal: A Turbo Pascal to Rust Transpiler
author: jjinux
body: Ruscal is a fairly-complete and well-tested Turbo Pascal to Rust transpiler, so you can run your old Turbo Pascal programs on modern computers. It supports mixing Rust and Turbo Pascal, embedding either way. It also supports graphics, including turtle graphics. I also included tools for pretty printing Turbo Pascal and converting old binary files to JSON. Great pain was taken to ensure accuracy with the original Turbo Pascal.

comments.author: jjinux
comments.text: Ruscal was written by Claude Code Opus with help from Claude Code Fable and a lot of input from me over a period of weeks. Claude wrote lots of programs to test behavior under Free Pascal and the original Turbo Pascal 7 running under DOSBox to ensure Ruscal ran with a high degree of accuracy. It's very well tested.I was able to run my original Turbo Pascal code, including graphics, and it was even able to read the binary files created by Turbo Pascal back in the day.

title: Show HN: 100ms copy-on-write workspaces for AI agents on macOS
author: gabrielfonseca
body:
# gabrielvfonseca/replica

Instant, disk-safe workspaces for AI agents on macOS. Clones a prebuilt project tree with APFS clonefile instead of checking out and installing.

- Stars: 1
- Forks: 0
- Watchers: 1
- Open issues: 0
- License: Other
- Default branch: main
- Created: 2026-10-25T19:38:05Z

## Languages

- Go Template
- JavaScript
- Makefile
- Ruby
- Rust
- Shell

## Topics

- agentic-workloads
- ai-agents
- apfs
- build-cache
- cleanup
- cli
- clonefile
- developer-tools
- fs
- macos
- rust
- sandbox
- workspace-manager

## Top Contributors

- gabrielvfonseca (57 contributions)
- dependabot[bot] (8 contributions)

---

## README

Replica Banner

# Isolated replicas of your workspace for AI agents

**Replica gives every agent run its own fully installed copy of your project, created in milliseconds with APFS copy-on-write. Each copy is a real git checkout, and automatic cleanup keeps total disk use bounded.**

```sh
cd "$(replica new --ttl 2h --name fix-login)"   # a ready workspace; the path goes to stdout
git checkout -b agent/fix-login && git commit -am "fix login" && git push -u origin agent/fix-login
replica rm <id>                                 # done; or let the TTL expire 
```

## Why

Agent workloads are dominated by creating and deleting small files (a checkout, 
`node_modules`, build output), and that's where macOS is slowest. A fresh
install takes seconds to minutes before the agent does any work.

Replica builds a **base** once: a git clone with its dependencies installed.
Each `replica new` clones that base with one `clonefile(2)` call. The data
blocks stay shared with the base until a file changes, so the new workspace is
ready almost at once. Measured on an Apple M1 Max, `replica new` of a 1,700-file
project takes about 100 ms at N = 1 and about 230 ms at N = 10 concurrent
workspaces, versus seconds for `git clone` plus an install. 
Numbers and methodology.

## What you get

- **Fast workspaces.** A clone of a 1,700-file project takes about 100 ms at N = 1 (about 230 ms with 10 concurrent workspaces), against seconds for `git clone` plus an install. Exact numbers vary with machine load; see docs/BENCHMARKS.md for the full table and methodology.
- **Real git.** Each workspace is a full git checkout. It can branch, commit, and push, and the base stays untouched. Details below.
- **Bounded disk.** TTL expiry, least-recently-used eviction, a byte cap, and an optional dedicated APFS volume with a quota.
- **Cheap updates.** `replica base refresh` brings the base up to date with its remote without a full rebuild. Details below.
- **Agent-ready.** A stable CLI with `--json` output, documented exit codes, and skills for Claude Code, Cursor, Copilot, Zed and Aider.
- **Concurrency tested.** `tests/concurrency.rs` runs 10 simultaneous `replica new`/use/`rm` cycles with zero SQLite busy errors, no corruption, and all workspaces created and removed. `replica gc` skips workspaces with a fresh lease (`.replica/lease`), so a launchd gc every 10 minutes never deletes a workspace an agent is using.

## Requirements

- macOS on an APFS volume. Replica uses `clonefile(2)`, which Linux does not provide. Tested on macOS 26.6 (Apple M1 Max).
- The base tree and every workspace must be on the **same APFS volume**. Clones cannot cross volumes, and Replica refuses rather than silently copying.

## Install

Binaries are published for macOS on Apple Silicon (`arm64`) and Intel (`x86_64`). A universal binary covers both.

```sh
# Homebrew is not available yet; see HOMEBREW.md.

# Installer script: verifies the download against sha256sums.txt
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/gabrielvfonseca/replica/main/scripts/get-replica.sh | sh

# From source (needs a Rust toolchain, https://rustup.rs)
git clone https://github.com/gabrielvfonseca/replica.git && cd replica
make release && PREFIX=$HOME/.local make install 
```

Run `replica help` for a guided overview, or `replica help quickstart` to get started.

## Quick start

**1. Choose a volume.** A dedicated APFS volume with a quota is the safest setup, because clones can never fill your main disk.

```sh
diskutil apfs list                                   # find your APFS container
./scripts/setup-volume.sh disk3 100g Work            # creates /Volumes/Work, turns off Spotlight indexing there
export REPLICA_ROOT=/Volumes/Work/replica 
```

Any APFS directory works too. Add `REPLICA_MAX_BYTES` to cap its size. See DISK_SAFETY for the trade-offs.

**2. Build a base once.**

```sh
replica base build --repo https://github.com/you/proj.git --setup "npm ci"
replica base check                                   # find build output that breaks when cloned 
```

**3. Create, use, and remove workspaces.**

```sh
cd "$(replica new --ttl 4h --name feature-x)"        # path on stdout, status on stderr
eval "$(replica env <id>)"                           # per-workspace TMPDIR and shared caches
replica touch <id>                                   # keep a long session out of LRU eviction
replica list                                         # table; add --json for scripts
replica rm <id>                                      # remove one (idempotent) 
```

**Branches with different lockfiles.** If you create a workspace from a branch
whose lockfile differs from the base, use `--ref`:

```sh
replica new --ref my-feature-branch 
```

Replica compares the branch's lockfile hash with the base's recorded hash. If
they match, the workspace is cloned directly (`cloned directly`). If they differ,
Replica clones the base, checks out `my-feature-branch`, then runs the setup
command (an incremental install) so the workspace gets correct dependencies, and
reports `lockfile drift on branch my-feature-branch; running incremental install`.
The CLI always tells you which path it took.

**4. Give your agents the skill.**

```sh
npx skills add gabrielvfonseca/replica               # skills.sh CLI: all six skills
replica setup --dry-run                              # see what setup would write for Claude Code, Cursor, Copilot, Zed, Aider
replica setup                                        # write it 
```

## Git: branch, commit, and push from a workspace

Yes. A workspace is a complete git repository, not a read-only copy:

| Operation | In a workspace | Effect on the base |
|---|---|---|
| `git checkout -b`, `git commit` | Works. Commits live in the workspace's `.git` | None |
| `git push origin ` | Works, to the remote the base was built from | None |
| `git pull`, `git fetch` | Works | None |
| `git status`, `git diff` | Works | None |

Things to know:

- **Remote credentials.** `push` uses whatever credentials git uses on this machine (SSH keys, a credential helper). Replica does not add or store any.
- **The remote is the one you built from.** `origin` in a workspace is the `--repo` you passed to `base build`. If that is a local path, pushes go to that path.
- **Workspaces are independent.** Two workspaces on the same branch will conflict on push, the same as two clones would. Use one branch per workspace.
- **Verified.** `tests/git_workspace.rs` builds a base from a bare repo, commits and pushes from a workspace, and checks that the origin and the base are as expected.

For agents that open pull requests, the flow is: `replica new`, work and commit on a branch, push, open the PR with `gh pr create`, then `replica rm`.

## Keeping the base fresh

When the remote moves on, `replica base refresh` updates the base. It does not rebuild from scratch:

1. Clonefiles the current base. This copies metadata only, so it is quick and uses almost no extra disk.
2. Runs `git fetch` and resets the copy to `origin/HEAD`. Only files that changed upstream are rewritten.
3. Re-runs setup **only if a lockfile changed**. If none did, setup is skipped entirely.
4. Swaps the new base in. Existing workspaces are unaffected, because each one owns its blocks.

So an upstream commit that does not touch dependencies costs a fetch and a checkout. A lockfile change costs about as much as the setup command itself. If the fast path fails for any reason, refresh falls back to a full rebuild.

Check freshness with `replica base status`, and use `replica new --require-fresh` to refuse a stale base.

## Disk usage: what a workspace really costs

- **At creation**, a workspace adds APFS metadata for every file and directory it contains. For the benchmark fixture (about 1,700 files) that is about 1.4 MB. Data blocks are shared with the base.
- **After the agent works**, every file it changes takes real space, because APFS copies the blocks that change. Rewriting 500 MB of build output costs 500 MB, and so does a `npm rebuild` that rewrites `node_modules`.
- **Deleting** a workspace frees only the blocks no other file shares. A fresh workspace frees little, and a heavily changed one frees much more.

This is why the TTL, LRU eviction, and byte cap exist. DISK_SAFETY explains each one.

Spotlight can also add writes on a busy volume. `scripts/setup-volume.sh` turns indexing off for the dedicated volume only (it needs `sudo`). We have not yet measured how much that changes benchmark results.

## Limitations

- **Path-dependent build output.** Some tools write absolute paths into their output: Python venvs, `node_modules/.bin` scripts, TypeScript `.tsbuildinfo`. These break in a clone. Run `replica base check` to find them, then fix them with `--post-clone` or by regenerating them. See the replica-base skill.
- **Cargo `target/` clones safely but adds cost.** A cloned `target/` gives a correct incremental no-op build (~20 ms, no recompile) when nothing changed, and recompiles only changed crates after a source touch — it does not force a full rebuild. However, `target/` is created by the setup command, so `.gitignore` does not keep it out of the base. Exclude it another way: either don't build `target/` during setup, or add an exclusion option to your base build. A cloned `target/` of a large project can add tens of MB of APFS metadata per clone, so exclude it if disk cost matters. A shared `CARGO_TARGET_DIR` under `$REPLICA_ROOT/cache` keeps incremental builds fast but reintroduces Cargo's file-lock waiting, so parallel agents can block on `Blocking waiting for file lock`. For parallel use, consider `sccache` instead of a shared target dir.
- **Cost scales with file count.** Each clone writes metadata for every file. Replica is much faster than copying or cloning file by file, but it is not free, and very large trees (hundreds of thousands of files) have not been measured.
- **Same volume only.** Source, base, and workspaces must share one APFS volume.
- **Not a speedup inside a running agent.** Replica makes workspace creation fast. It does not speed up reads or writes during a run, does not reduce the RAM or CPU used by running many agents at once, and does not fix Spotlight or XProtect scanning.
- **macOS only.** Linux and Windows are out of scope.

## Benchmarks

The suite in `benchmarks/` compares `replica new` with 
`git clone` plus install, `git worktree` plus install, `pnpm` with the global
virtual store, and `cp -c`, and it also measures `replica rm` and 
`replica base refresh`, at concurrency N = 1, 5, and 10.

```sh
make release                                         # target/release/replica
make bench                                           # bundled fixture (~15 min)
make bench CONCURRENCY=1,5,10                        # parallel workspace creation 
```

Full results, methodology, machine details, and exact commands are in 
docs/BENCHMARKS.md.

Headline (Apple M1 Max, macOS 26.6.2, under load, 1,739-file npm project):

| Concurrency | `replica new` median | `cp -c -R` median | `git clone` + setup median |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| N = 1 | ~100 ms | ~958 ms | ~3.96 s |
| N = 10 (all at once) | ~230 ms | ~3.55 s | ~4 s |

`replica new` is about 15x faster than `cp -c -R` even with 10 concurrent
workspaces, and tens of times faster than `git clone` plus an install. The
one-time `replica base build` (~2–3 s) is less than a single `git clone` +
setup, so Replica comes out ahead on the very first workspace.

- **2026-11-09, under load** (1-minute load 171–184 on 10 cores). These
 absolute times are inflated by the shared machine load; relative ordering
 held, but do not quote the ratios as settled. Exact numbers and P95 values
 are in docs/BENCHMARKS.md.
- **2026-10-25, quiet machine** (previous harness, 1,842 files): `replica new`
 66 ms, `git clone` + setup 3.10 s, `cp -c` 1.33 s. Different harness and
 fixture; not directly comparable to the 2026-11-09 run.

Replica adds APFS metadata per file per clone (~1.4 MB for a 1,700-file project
on a quiet machine); data blocks are shared with the base and changed files cost
real space as the agent works. The replica-benchmarks skill lists what a clean run needs.

## Development

```sh
make help              # every target
make check             # fmt, clippy (warnings are errors), and tests; what CI runs
make bench             # benchmark suite
make dist              # release binaries in bin/ 
```

CI runs on GitHub Actions macOS runners. CONTRIBUTING.md covers the workflow, and AGENTS.md holds the rules for coding agents. The replica-dev skill describes the code layout.

## Docs

| | |
|---|---|
| CLI | Every command, flag, output, and exit code |
| SPEC | Problem, goals, non-goals, requirements |
| ARCHITECTURE | Components, layout, and flows |
| DATA_MODEL | SQLite schema, state machine, migrations |
| DISK_SAFETY | Quotas, TTL, eviction, caches, and what deleting frees |
| BENCHMARKS | Methodology, results, and corrections |
| benchmarks/ | The benchmark suite and fixture project |
| skills/ | Agent skills: usage, base, maintenance, development, benchmarks, release |
| ROADMAP | Shipped work, next steps, open questions |
| CHANGELOG | Notable changes by version |
